name: Document databases
summary: Records stored as JSON documents that the database can query, index and update field by field.
howItWorks: A document database stores each record as a self-contained document, usually JSON or a binary form of it such as MongoDB’s BSON, grouped into collections. Like a key-value store it can fetch a document by its ID, but it also understands what’s inside. You can filter on any field, including nested objects and arrays, index those fields, change one field without rewriting the rest, and run aggregations. Documents in one collection don’t need the same fields, so the shape can change without a migration, and most databases can still validate documents against a schema if you want one. Data that’s read together, such as an order and its line items, usually lives in one document, so reading it is one lookup, but data shared between documents gets copied or linked by ID, and joins across collections are limited. To scale out, a collection is split across shards by a shard key: a query that includes the key goes to one shard, and one that doesn’t goes to all of them.
analogy: A filing cabinet of complete forms, one folder per customer. The clerk can pull every folder where the city is Oslo, and new forms can gain boxes without reprinting the old ones.
useWhen: Records with nested, varying fields: product catalogs, user profiles, content
Data that’s read and written as one object, like an order with its line items
Apps whose data shape changes often, especially when the code already works in JSON
avoidWhen: Data with many relationships, queried from every side; joins across collections are limited
Work that needs transactions across many records all the time; they exist, but cost more than single-document writes
example: An online shop keeps each product as one MongoDB document: name, price, a `specs` object whose fields differ between laptops and shoes, and an array of sizes with stock counts. An index on `specs.brand` serves the brand filter, and a price change is one `$set` on one field. A monthly report joining products with orders and returns, though, is easier in SQL.

providers.aws: Amazon DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible); DynamoDB also stores JSON documents
providers.azure: Azure Cosmos DB, with its own NoSQL API or a MongoDB-compatible one
providers.oss: MongoDB (SSPL, source-available), Apache CouchDB, FerretDB (MongoDB-compatible, on PostgreSQL), ArangoDB (BSL, also a graph database); PostgreSQL’s `jsonb` for documents inside a relational database

diagram.caption: The collection is sharded by user ID. Lookups that include it (colored by key) go to the one shard that holds that user. A search on another field, such as city, can’t know where matches live, so the router sends it to every shard and merges the answers.

story: By the mid-2000s, web applications passed data around as JSON, which Douglas Crockford described in RFC 4627 in 2006, while relational databases made developers split every object into rows across tables and join them back together. In April 2005 Damien Katz, who had worked on Lotus Notes at IBM, started CouchDB: a database of JSON documents with a schema-free design, read and written over HTTP. It became a top-level Apache project in November 2008.

MongoDB, built at 10gen, had its first official release in February 2009. It kept the JSON-like documents but added what developers expected from a database, such as queries on any field, secondary indexes and in-place updates. Later releases filled in what the early versions left out, including the WiredTiger storage engine, acquired in 2014, and multi-document ACID transactions in 2018.

The model then spread beyond MongoDB itself. In October 2018 MongoDB moved to the SSPL, aimed at companies offering it as a service, and in January 2019 AWS launched DocumentDB, its own MongoDB-compatible service. Relational databases met documents halfway: PostgreSQL 9.4 added the indexable `jsonb` type in 2014. Today the same JSON record can live in a document database, a relational one or DynamoDB.

choices.why: Applications already worked with nested objects. Keeping an object and its parts in one document removed the mapping to tables and made reading it a single lookup.
Each document can have its own fields, so a new field ships with the code instead of waiting for a migration. Optional schema validation lets teams add the guarantees back where they want them.

choices.choice: Shard by a key the developer chooses
choices.why: Splitting a collection across servers by a shard key lets the cluster grow, and queries that name the key stay on one shard. Choosing that key well is the big design decision.
